subtype: Approach: researching the person before writing [Thinking]
passage: In the university library in Toronto, Siddiq wanted to write to Amara, an engineer at a mapping company he admired. He almost typed "Hi, I'd love to work at your firm", then stopped and opened her profile instead. Her posts were mostly about routing delivery vans. Then he found a recorded talk she had given at a local meetup, about handling roads that closed suddenly. He watched it twice with headphones on and noted one thing she said: that real maps are always slightly wrong. His message became: "Your talk on road closures made me wonder how you decide when to trust old data. Would you have two minutes to point me to one thing to read?" He read it aloud once, and sent it.

qa.q: What was Amara's talk about?
qa.a: Amara's talk was about handling roads that closed suddenly.

qa.q: What is Siddiq feeling as he stops before sending the first draft?
qa.a: Siddiq feels cautious and thoughtful, realising that a generic line would waste her attention and choosing to prepare.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Siddiq add, and why?
qa.a: Siddiq could look for a mutual contact who could introduce him, because a warm introduction can make even a good message easier to answer.

qa.q: How might Amara see this message?
qa.a: Amara sees a question about her own talk and a small request, which shows the sender did real reading and makes a reply easier to write.

grounding: Shows researching a stranger's posts and talk before writing so that the message asks something specific and respectful.

subtype: Approach: short specific message with a small ask [Action]
passage: I share a flat with Vasudha, so I was there when she wrote to the alumnus. She had read his profile for a whole evening, then wrote only four lines. First: who she is, a third-year student. Second: a sentence about his article on reading logs, which she said helped her project. Third: "Would you be open to a call of fifteen minutes, or, if easier, one question by message?" Fourth: thanks. She read it aloud to me and cut two lines that sounded too eager. I do not know if she was nervous; she kept tapping her pen. She sent it at nine. By noon the next day he had answered with a time on Saturday. — Siddharth

qa.q: How many lines did Vasudha write in the message?
qa.a: Vasudha wrote only four lines.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have felt while sending the message, judging from what Siddharth saw?
qa.a: Vasudha may have felt nervous, since she kept tapping her pen, though Siddharth says this is only a guess.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vasudha use if there is no reply, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could send one polite follow-up after a week, because a busy person may simply have missed the first message.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth to watch Vasudha write the message?
qa.a: Siddharth hears the message read aloud and sees the pen-tapping but cannot read Vasudha's mind, so Siddharth stays careful about guessing the feelings.

grounding: Shows a very short message with who the sender is, one specific compliment, and a small easy-to-answer request.

subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of the call [Thinking]
passage: The call with the alumnus was at 5 p.m. and Varun had been pacing his room since lunch. His flatmate Chinmay watched him mutter. "Are you talking to yourself?" "Practising." Varun had a note card: opening line, "Thank you for making time; I read your article on delivery planning." Then two questions: "How did you pick your first project?" and "What would you do differently?" He also imagined the worst: a long silence on the line. What would he say? He decided: "Take your time, I have another question ready." Seeing it coming made silence feel like a pause, not a disaster. At 4:55 his hands were cold, but not shaking. When the call started, he said the first line as planned.

qa.q: What time was Varun's call with the alumnus?
qa.a: The call was at 5 p.m.

qa.q: What is Varun feeling as the call approaches?
qa.a: Varun feels nervous, with cold hands, but steadier than before because he has rehearsed for the awkward moments.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Varun add, and why?
qa.a: Varun could do a mock call with Chinmay asking surprising questions, because rehearsing alone cannot reproduce a real person's unexpected turns.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see Varun's practice?
qa.a: Chinmay watches Varun mutter and asks if he is talking to himself, so Chinmay may find it odd at first but learns it is a plan.

grounding: Shows mentally rehearsing an opening line and questions and imagining a silence so that the real call feels less threatening.

subtype: Approach: asking for a job in the first message [Pitfall]
passage: Ishita, let old Kavitha tell you about the worst message I ever sent. I was twenty. I found a director at a big firm on a professional site, and my whole message was: "Hello sir, I am a final-year student looking for a job. Please refer me." Nothing else. No name of my college, no reason why him, no question. I waited two weeks and heard nothing, and I felt insulted. Later, when I was on the other side and receiving such messages, I understood. I did not know who this person was and could not tell if the student was any good. A referral is a favour to someone you trust. I had sent him a request with no relationship behind it.

qa.q: How old was Kavitha when the message was sent?
qa.a: Kavitha was twenty.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling after two weeks without a reply?
qa.a: Kavitha felt insulted and ignored, before later understanding why the message had no answer.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kavitha have used, and why?
qa.a: Kavitha could have written a short note that said who Kavitha was and asked one question about the director's work, because trust must start before a favour like a referral.

qa.q: How would the director have seen that message?
qa.a: The director would see a stranger with no name of a college, no reason for choosing them and no question, so there was nothing to trust or answer.

grounding: Shows asking a stranger for a referral in the very first message and receiving no answer for lack of any relationship.

subtype: Approach: avoidance out of fear of bothering people [Pitfall]
passage: Three drafts sat in Arohi's message folder, each started and none sent. The internship applications closed in two weeks, and her friend Raghav had already had three calls. "Just send one," he said from the doorway. "They're senior people. They're busy. It'll annoy them," said Arohi. She had rewritten the same three lines forty times. Every evening she opened the folder, added a comma, and closed it. She imagined an engineer reading it between meetings and sighing. Eleven days later, Raghav's chat lit up with a referral from someone he had written to on a whim. Arohi looked at her own folder. Three drafts, and no conversations, and only three days left.

qa.q: How many drafts were in Arohi's message folder?
qa.a: Three drafts sat in Arohi's message folder.

qa.q: What is Arohi feeling as she opens the folder each evening?
qa.a: Arohi feels anxious and afraid of bothering people, adding a comma and closing the folder again.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Arohi try with only three days left, and why?
qa.a: Arohi could send one short message with a small ask today, because a polite request costs a stranger little and silence gives no chance at all.

qa.q: How does Raghav see Arohi's hesitation?
qa.a: Raghav urges her to just send one, having already had calls and a referral, so Raghav sees sending as lower risk than Arohi does.

grounding: Shows drafting messages to professionals but never sending them out of fear of being a nuisance, so no conversations happen while a deadline nears.

subtype: Approach: going through a mutual connection [Action]
passage: Keerthana, you asked how I got the reply from the analyst. Honestly I had written to her cold two weeks before and heard nothing. Then in a lecture, Prof. Menon mentioned a former student who now works in the same team. Something clicked. After class I asked, "Ma'am, is it the same person? Would you be comfortable introducing me? Just one line, please." She smiled, said "Send me two lines about what you want," and I did. That evening she forwarded my note with a friendly message on top. The analyst replied in a day, "Any friend of Prof. Menon's, happy to talk." I'm Anjali, and I have learned that a warm door beats a cold email.

qa.q: What did Prof. Menon ask Anjali to send?
qa.a: Prof. Menon asked Anjali to send two lines about what Anjali wanted.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling after two weeks of silence from the analyst?
qa.a: Anjali was disappointed and a little discouraged, until the lecture comment made something click.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Anjali use if the professor could not help, and why?
qa.a: Anjali could look for a shared club or former classmate who knows the analyst, because any mutual contact can make the first contact warmer.

qa.q: How might Prof. Menon see the request?
qa.a: Prof. Menon is asked politely for a one-line introduction, gets two lines about the goal and forwards it, so the professor probably sees a student who is easy to help.

grounding: Shows using a mutual contact, a professor, for an introduction that earns a warmer reply than a cold message.

passage: Gopika, since you keep telling me you don't want to be pushy, let old Ujjwal tell you about my rule. When I was twenty-one I wrote to an engineer and heard nothing. I did not know whether to write again or drop it. I stayed awake over it. Then a senior said, "Make a rule beforehand, so your head doesn't argue." Mine was: if there is no answer in a week, I send one short, polite follow-up. After that, I let it go and think no worse of anyone. A week passed. I sent two lines: "Just checking that my message did not get buried. No worries if the timing is bad." No reply. I closed the tab and felt calm. Three months later that same engineer nodded to me at a conference and said, "Sorry, I missed it. Ask me now."

qa.q: How long did Ujjwal's rule say to wait before following up?
qa.a: Ujjwal's rule said to wait a week.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling before the rule was made?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt unsettled and stuck, unsure whether to write again and lying awake over it.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept Ujjwal calm after no reply, and why?
qa.a: Ujjwal made the rule beforehand and closed the tab once it was used, because the decision was already made and there was nothing left to argue with oneself about.

qa.q: How might the engineer have seen the follow-up?
qa.a: The engineer received a short, polite note with no pressure, which may explain the friendly remark at the conference months later.

grounding: Shows an if-then plan for following up once after a week and then moving on without resentment.

subtype: Approach: reciprocity by offering something useful [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Thinking about what I can offer

Hi Uma,

I was about to write to Dr Rao again with another "please guide me". Then I stopped, because what do I give him? He is busy, and what I want is all take. So here is my plan. He has an open-source tool for cleaning survey data, and there is a bug list. I will actually try it on my own project, note any confusing steps, and send him two clear pages. I also went to the workshop last week; I can send my notes from the sessions he missed. Hopefully it helps and starts a proper conversation. What do you think? Is that presumptuous?

Rukmini

qa.q: What will Rukmini try on the project?
qa.a: Rukmini will try the open-source tool for cleaning survey data on the project.

qa.q: What is Rukmini feeling as the email is written?
qa.a: Rukmini feels hopeful but a bit unsure, ending with a question about whether the plan is presumptuous.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rukmini use if the offer is ignored, and why?
qa.a: Rukmini could join the tool's public discussion and answer a beginner's question, because helping in public shows the same goodwill without needing a private reply.

qa.q: How might Dr Rao see this offer?
qa.a: Dr Rao would receive two clear pages about his own tool from a real user, which gives something useful instead of another request for guidance.

grounding: Shows building a relationship on what one can give, such as testing a tool or sharing notes, instead of only asking.

subtype: Approach: reviewing what went wrong after silence [Revision]
passage: Himani's fest was in three weeks, and she needed a sponsor's contact. She had sent five messages to alumni and got five silences. On Thursday she sat with Irfan, a senior in her hostel, and slid her laptop across. He read one draft for a minute. "This is a wall," he said gently. "Three paragraphs, all about the fest history, and I still can't tell what you're asking." Another said: "I would love guidance regarding possible opportunities." "Opportunities for what?" Irfan asked. Himani laughed, then winced. They cut it to four lines: who she is, why this person, one clear question about a sponsorship call. She sent three of the rewritten ones that night. By Saturday, two answered.

qa.q: How many silences did Himani get before she showed Irfan?
qa.a: She got five silences.

qa.q: What is Himani feeling when Irfan calls the draft a wall?
qa.a: Himani laughs and then winces, so she feels embarrassed but amused, and she accepts the honest feedback.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Himani use to test the rewrite, and why?
qa.a: Himani could read it aloud to a friend and ask what the request is, because if the friend cannot say, the message is still unclear.

qa.q: How does Irfan see the drafts?
qa.a: Irfan reads for a minute and says gently that they are long and vague, so Irfan sees a fixable problem and helps cut it down.

grounding: Shows getting a senior's review after repeated silence, seeing the drafts were long and vague, and rewriting them shorter with better results.

subtype: Approach: keeping a simple contact log [Action]
passage: Santosh opened a plain spreadsheet in his Delhi flat and made five columns: name, date, what we talked about, what I promised, follow-up date. He typed in his first row from last week's call with Chandrika, a product manager: 12 March, hiring for the data team, sent her an article, follow up after Diwali. Four more rows followed from his notes. Every Sunday he opened the sheet, wrote thank-you messages to the week's contacts, and set reminders. Two months later, when Chandrika mentioned an opening, he wrote back, "Since we talked in March about the data team, I remembered you were looking for interns." It read like a friend, not a stranger, and it was true because the sheet had kept it.

qa.q: Which five items did Santosh put in the columns?
qa.a: He used name, date, what we talked about, what I promised, and follow-up date.

qa.q: What is Santosh probably feeling when he opens the sheet on Sundays?
qa.a: Santosh is probably steady and purposeful, since he is turning scattered conversations into tidy follow-ups.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Santosh add, and why?
qa.a: Santosh could occasionally share something useful without waiting for a reason, because a log keeps track of contacts but goodwill grows from small gifts too.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see the message about the opening?
qa.a: Chandrika receives a note that recalls their March talk and her own interest in interns, so it feels personal and not like a mass message.

grounding: Shows keeping a simple record of each conversation with follow-up dates and thanking people afterwards so that single chats become lasting contacts.
